data.title: Subtree of Another Tree
data.summary:
Input: Two binary trees, root and subRoot.
Output: A boolean indicating if subRoot is a subtree of root.
Rules: A subtree of root is a tree consisting of a node in root and all of its descendants. The structure and node values must match exactly.
constraints: The number of nodes in the root tree is in the range [1, 2000].
The number of nodes in the subRoot tree is in the range [1, 1000].
Node values are in the range [-10^4, 10^4].

data.generator_code:
def list_to_tree(lst):
    if not lst:
        return None
    root = TreeNode(lst[0])
    queue = [root]
    i = 1
    while queue and i < len(lst):
        curr = queue.pop(0)
        if i < len(lst) and lst[i] is not None:
            curr.left = TreeNode(lst[i])
            queue.append(curr.left)
        i += 1
        if i < len(lst) and lst[i] is not None:
            curr.right = TreeNode(lst[i])
            queue.append(curr.right)
        i += 1
    return root

def generate(rng, n):
    root_vals = [rng.randint(-10, 10) for _ in range(min(n, 50))]
    sub_size = max(1, min(n // 2, 10))
    sub_vals = root_vals[:sub_size]
    return [list_to_tree(root_vals), list_to_tree(sub_vals)]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    root_vals = [1] * min(n, 50)
    sub_vals = [1] * min(n // 2, 25)
    return [list_to_tree(root_vals), list_to_tree(sub_vals)]

data.key_insight: A tree subRoot is a subtree of root if subRoot is identical to root, or identical to any subtree of root's left or right children.

steps.title: Handle Base Cases
steps.detail: If subRoot is None, it is technically a subtree of any tree (return True). If root is None, subRoot cannot be a subtree (return False).

steps.title: Check Identity
steps.detail: Check if the tree rooted at root is identical to subRoot using a helper function.

steps.title: Recursive Search
steps.detail: If not identical, recursively check if subRoot is a subtree of root.left or root.right.

events.detail: Pattern: Tree Traversal and Comparison · 3 hints

data.pattern_summary: Visiting every node in a main structure and performing a full structural check at each node to see if a smaller structure matches.

pattern_options.name: Tree Traversal and Comparison
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to visit each node in the main tree and check if the tree rooted at that node matches the target tree.

pattern_options.name: Binary Search Tree Property
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. The problem does not state that the trees are ordered binary search trees, so we cannot use node values to navigate.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers are used for linear data structures like arrays or strings, not hierarchical tree structures.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A hash map does not help preserve or check the hierarchical parent-child relationships required for tree structures.

signals.phrase: Two binary trees, root and subRoot
signals.hint: Implies we are comparing two separate hierarchical structures.

signals.phrase: a subtree of root is a tree consisting of a node in root and all of its descendants
signals.hint: Indicates we must check potential matches starting from every possible node in the main tree.

signals.phrase: structure and node values must match exactly
signals.hint: Tells us we need a helper function to compare two trees node by node.

data.brute_force_idea: Traverse every node of the root tree. At each node, run a full comparison against the subRoot tree to check if they are identical.
data.brute_force_why: In the worst case, for every one of the m nodes in the root tree, we traverse up to n nodes in the subRoot tree to compare them.
data.bottleneck: Calling the tree comparison function at every single node of the root tree, which leads to redundant checks.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times the comparison function is invoked relative to the nodes in the main tree.
Notice that every node in the root tree becomes a starting candidate for a full tree comparison.
Consider whether we visit the same subtrees multiple times during the recursive traversal.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The optimized solution avoids repeating redundant sub-checks by combining a full tree traversal of the main tree with a structural comparison helper whenever a node matches. Instead of a single monolithic pass, it systematically visits every node in the root tree and triggers a comparison function that checks down the height of the subRoot.

derivation.note: Triggers the comparison check at each of the N nodes in the root tree.
Recurses down the left and right branches of the root tree.
Compares every node in the subRoot tree of size M when a match is attempted.

data.time_summary: Visiting each of the N nodes in the root tree takes O(N) operations. At each node, if the values match, we potentially compare up to M nodes of the subRoot tree, taking O(M) time. Multiplying these gives O(N * M) total time complexity.
data.space_summary: The space complexity is determined by the maximum call stack depth, which corresponds to the height (H) of the tree. In the worst case of a skewed tree, this is O(N); in a balanced tree, it is O(log N).
data.takeaway: When checking for structural containment between two trees, traverse the larger structure and invoke a secondary helper function to validate the exact match at each candidate node.
mistakes: Forgetting to handle cases where either root or subRoot is initially empty or None.
Assuming tree equality can be checked with simple value comparisons without verifying left and right child pointers.
Confusing the size of the main tree (N) and the subtree (M) when calculating the worst-case runtime complexity.

data.overview: The algorithm checks if subRoot matches the current root node using an exact tree comparison function. If it doesn't match, it recursively checks the left and right subtrees of root.
data.intuition: Imagine checking every single room in a house (root) to see if it matches a blueprint of a smaller cottage (subRoot). You enter each room, compare it thoroughly, and if it fails, you look deeper into the left and right corridors.
